name: Lena Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Lena, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grid upgrade crew, which is a bit different from the normal fault crews. We go out along the existing lines and fit automatic reclosers, fault sensors and little radio boxes, so the control room can see problems and switch power around without sending a truck. Most days it's two or three poles, a lot of careful wiring at height, then testing with the control room on the phone. I love that the network gets cleverer every week, and what wears me out is waiting an hour for control to confirm a test.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I moved here eight months ago for this job, into a shared flat with a friend, Ines, who's a nurse. The deposit and the move ate my savings, so I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank. I use AI tools every day, for wiring diagrams, for studying, for planning my budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but the grid still needs upgrading either way. I'd probably post something like the sensors don't care about hype. I'd keep using the tools I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau could actually hurt my crew. A lot of the upgrade money came in because the company wanted a smart grid to go with all the AI talk. If the hype dies, the board might cut the programme, and the upgrade crew is the newest, so we'd be first to be folded back into fault work, with less overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my skills sharp and keep doing extra courses online, so I'm useful on any crew. I'd try to rebuild a month of savings by spring. And I'd ask my supervisor straight out how safe the upgrade budget is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about robots, about budgets and being the new person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose if you went back to fault work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some overtime, and the interesting work. Money-wise maybe a hundred a month less. But it's still a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel safe as the newest on the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not entirely. Last in, first out is how it usually goes. That's why I'd want to be the one who knows the most about the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for grid work. More data, more sensors, more need for people who understand both the poles and the software. I'd post about it and probably get some eye-rolls from the fault crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm well placed. The planning and paperwork goes to software, which I'd happily hand over, and the network gets more automated, which is literally my job. The climbing stays for years because robots spread slowly in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to train as a commissioning tech, the person who sets up and tests the automation from the ground. I'd use AI tools to study for the certificate at night. And I'd volunteer to show the older crews how to use the new tablets, so I'm the go-to person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like the future is heading my way for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the older crews resent people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few do. Big Pete, one of the older lineworkers, calls me the laptop girl. When his tablet freezes, Big Pete still comes to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money? Still two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, so I'd be careful. But a commissioning role pays a grade higher, so if I got it I'd be saving properly by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move fast and get people trained, not just complain. I'd be pushing the company to retrain crews as robot supervisors and commissioning techs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's scary but not hopeless for me. The control room and planning go almost straight away in 2028. By 2031 robots climb, so my hands-on part goes, but someone still has to set up, test and fix the automation. I'd be 30 and I'd need to be that someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard on training from day one, every course the company offers and online stuff at night. I'd move to wherever the robot test sites are, even another region, since I've only just moved here anyway. And I'd keep my spending tight to build a bit of a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but determined. Like the first time I did a live-line test with control on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there aren't enough of those jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be one of many fighting for them. That's what worries me. I can be good at the automation work, but not everyone gets a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move again so soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I've got no kids, no mortgage. Ines would understand. I'd miss her, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a real plan, and people should start now. I'd tell my crew to take every training chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good timing for me. The thinking side goes in 2031, robots in 2034. I'd be 32, with seven years to build a career in automation and some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the commissioning certificate in the first year, then learn robot maintenance. I'd save two months of money by 2028. I'd also try to get on the company's robot pilot team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly hopeful. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company might outsource the robots to some big tech firm and not need its own techs. That would be bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push back if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'm not a big union person, but I'd join if they were fighting to keep the work in-house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and the grid will need more skilled people, not fewer. I'd be upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's my favourite picture. Robots come about 2039, and I'd be 40 and probably leading an automation team by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the courses at a steady pace, save, and maybe do a part-time engineering degree. I'd use AI to help with the study. I'd also look at a small investment in a local renewable project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It feels like a good decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about this one hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only money in the first couple of years. Two weeks saved isn't a lot. But I'd get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the software as well as the spanners. That's what I'd tell my younger self.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be a scramble for the few new jobs. What would help is companies training their own people first, and pay that lets you study without going broke.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women. The new tech roles could be a way in for more women in the trade, if companies don't just hire the usual faces.

Oddly, AI Plateau worries her because her **upgrade budget** could be cut.
She's **calm** in slow pictures and **anxious** at AGI by 2028.
